newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army says it killed 51 Hutu rebels.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army says it killed 51 Hutu rebels.

text.p: Burundi's army said on Friday troops killed 51 Hutu rebels near the capital Bujumbura and in the south while diplomats said a Swiss nun was killed in a mine explosion.
The United States meanwhile said it was very concerned at the recent surge of violence and condemned rebel attacks on unarmed civilians and government reprisals against other defenceless targets.
Diplomats said the Swiss nun, Claudine-Germaine Buchwolder, was killed on Thursday when her vehicle set off an anti-tank mine near her home in Mutambu commune 20 km (12 miles) south of the capital.
They said she had worked in Burundi for the last two years.

An army spokesman said eight rebels were killed at Gaereni in the south on Thursday and another 40 were killed in hills when they were hunted down by troops. A total of seven weapons were seized, he added.
He said rebels also attacked Mimago village near Bujumbura and killed an old woman before troops killed three of them.
Officials in the south said funerals would be held on Friday for 43 seminary school students and their teachers killed by rebels in an attack at Buta village in the south on Wednesday.
Another 40 students were wounded in the school attack.
In Geneva, the United Nations said on Friday dozens of people were dying daily in new violence in south Burundi, where the Tutsi-dominated army is at war with majority Hutu rebels.
In a statement released by the U.S. embassy in Burundi, the State Department said the U.S. government sent its condolences to the families of the dead in Buta but warned against revenge attacks.

"We understand that some may be contemplating avenging this heinous act. Using this massacre as justification for additional bloodshed will only serve to prolong the violence," the U.S. statement said.
It said the international community and most Burundians regarded all violence against unarmed civilians and dispicable.
"The United States government once again calls on all the parties to the conflict in Burundi to disavow acts of violence against the population.

"We also call on the security services, the (rebel) CNDD and other belligerent parties to exercise strong leadership and discipline to prevent further tragedies," said the statement, which reiterated calls for an end to hostilities and the start of negotiations to return Burundi to constitutional order.
"Security for all Burundians will only come from negotiations and compromise," the U.S. statement said.
U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut said in Geneva on Friday the violence in the southern regions of Bururi and Makamba had displaced large numbers of civilians but she gave no details.

The army, which grabbed power in a coup last year, announced earlier this week that it had killed at least 300 Hutu rebels in Bururi since April 5 for the loss of six soldiers after it said a force of up to 3,000 rebels attacked from bases in Tanzania.
More than 150,000 people, mostly civilians, have been killed in massacres and civil war between the Tutsi-dominated army and rebels since troops killed Burundi's first Hutu president in 1993.
Burundian Hutu rebels of the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) were uprooted from bases in Zaire last year when Zairean Tutsi-dominated rebels seized the area.
